title: Diurnal effects of dynamic lighting on alertness, cognition, and mood of mentally fatigued individuals in a daylight deprived environment
research_question: This study investigated the non-image forming (NIF) effects of dynamic light on alertness, cognitive performance and mood on mental fatigue, as well as moderation of task difficulty in lighting perception.

participants.description: 16 college students (8 males, 8 females) aged 22–26 years (mean age=24) with science and engineering majors (excluding lighting), no eye complaints/color vision deficiencies, no drinking/smoking, no jet lag/night shift in the month prior, non-extreme chronotypes (MEQ), no sleep problems (PSQI≤7). Participants maintained regular work and rest cycles (wake-up: 07.00-09.00 am, bed: 10.00 pm-12.00 am).
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated, but implies recruitment from a university setting.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Confined lit room (3m x 2m x 2.8m) with white walls. Two lighting conditions: 1. Static Lighting (SL): CCT maintained at 4000K. 2. Dynamic Lighting (DL): CCT ranged from 4000K to 12000K in a linear function, with 16-step changes (500K increments), each step lasting 94 seconds (except 4000K/12000K which lasted 47s). A full cycle (increase then decrease) took 50 minutes. Illuminance was kept constant at approximately 500 lx on the desk for both conditions. CRI ≥ 80, no perceived flickering. Melanopic EDI for 4000K was 224 lx, for 12000K was 420 lx.

measures.instrument: Positive Affect and Negative Affect Scale (PANAS) (Chinese version)

measures.construct: Mental fatigue (alertness, energetic, sleepy, vigour, fatigue, depression, confusion, tension, anger)
measures.instrument: Visual Analog Scales (VAS) (8 items, 10-point Likert) and Brunel Mood Scale (BRUMS) (6 subscales, 4 items each, 5-point Likert)
Multi-Attribute Task Battery-II (MATB-II) (low, medium, high difficulty levels)
National Aeronautics Space Administration Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) and task rating scale (10-point Likert)
Event-related potentials (ERPs) - P300 amplitude and latency (at Fz, Cz, Pz, Oz electrodes)

findings.quote: no significant main or interaction effect for P300 latency at any electrode site

findings.mechanism: Daytime light exposure, regardless of dynamic or static, did not significantly alter melatonin secretion, suggesting other NIF mechanisms are at play for alertness effects.
findings.quote: no significant difference in the salivary melatonin levels between SL and DL conditions (F1,48=2.53, p>0.05, R2=0.11)

findings.antecedent: Testing period (before vs. after light exposure)
findings.mechanism: Melatonin levels did not significantly change across the testing period.
findings.quote: did not differ across testing period (F1,48=3.71, p>0.05, R2=0.11)

findings.mechanism: No interaction effect between lighting condition and testing period on melatonin levels.
findings.quote: did not show a significant interaction effect of lighting condition and testing period (F1,48=0.01, p>0.05, R2=0.11)

mechanisms: Dynamic light may contribute to alertness recovery by maintaining vigilance at baseline levels, possibly through higher CCT or light dynamics activating arousal levels, rather than melatonin suppression.
Dynamic light improves working memory and executive control by increasing attentional resources allocated to tasks, as indicated by larger P300 amplitudes.
Dynamic light provides a more comfortable atmosphere perception, which helps maintain positive mood and inhibit negative mood in fatigued individuals.
Dynamic light reduces perceived physical demand and frustration during cognitive tasks, contributing to better performance.
implementation_implications: Dynamic lighting could be applied to improve alertness, cognitive performance, and positive mood of fatigued individuals in isolated, confined, and extreme (ICE) environments with daylight deprivation.
Appropriate dynamic light manipulation can provide comfortable atmosphere perception and help meet demands for stress recovery in long-term and stressful work settings.

tables.description: Photometric parameters at eye level for the typical lighting conditions (4000K, 6000K, 8000K, 12000K), including illuminance, CCT, total irradiance, CRI, and spectrally weighted a-opic irradiances (Melanopsin, S-cone, M-cone, L-cone, Rods).
Statistics of PSQI and MEQ scores for the test participants (Min, Max, Mean, Standard deviation).
The MATB-II with three difficulty levels, specifying events/minute for SYSMON, update/response for TRACK, and pump failures/minute for RESMAN, along with duration.

Results of the LMM analyses for VAS and BRUMS scores across baseline, first fatigue induction, and second fatigue induction, including EMM ± SD, F-statistic, df, p-value, R-squared, and post-hoc comparisons.

Results of the LMM analyses for subjective measures (Subjective sleepiness, Positive mood, Negative mood) under Baseline, Static Lighting, and Dynamic Lighting conditions, including EMM ± SD, F-statistic, p-value, and R-squared.

limitations: Compliance with the imposed sleep-wake schedule for the nights before the experimental session was not monitored (e.g., using actigraphy or sleep diaries).

The study provides preliminary support for DL advantages in countering mental fatigue, but practical applications are complex and multidimensional; future studies should manipulate multi-dimensional fatigue levels.
Sex differences were not tested due to the study focus and small sample size.

paper_metadata.title: Effects of dynamic lighting on office workers: First results of a field study with monthly alternating settings
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Effects of dynamic lighting on office workers: First results of a field study with monthly alternating settings
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Dynamic lighting is designed to have positive effects on well-being and performance. In a field experiment we tested whether these effects are detectable and stable over time when employed in actual work settings. The study consists of two tranches, one following a monthly alternating experimental design, the other a yearly alternating one. This paper reports on the first tranche. In a dual balanced design, office workers experienced dynamic or static lighting according to an a-b-a /b-a-b scheme over three consecutive periods (N = 142, 90, 83). Questionnaire data suggest no significant differences for need for recovery, vitality, alertness, headache and eyestrain, mental health, sleep quality, or subjective performance, although employees were more satisfied with the dynamic lighting. Implications and limitations of the study are discussed.
